name: Longest stretch of mostly winning days
brief:
`pnl` is a trader's daily P&L in pounds. A day with a profit above £0 is a winning day; any other day is a losing day. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive days with strictly more winning days than losing days, or 0 if there is none.

Write `longest_winning_stretch(pnl)`.

Example. For `[-4, 6, 0, 2, -1, -3]` the first five days hold 2 winning days and 3 losing days. Days 1 to 3 hold 2 wins and 1 loss, and no run of 4 or more has more wins. So the answer is 3.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 100{,}000$ days, each a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Trying every start and end day is too slow.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Score a winning day +1 and any other day -1, and keep a running score. A run ending today wins when the score then exceeds the score before it began. If the score is not positive, which earlier score would you look for, and why is its first time the one you want?

examples.note: Days 1 to 3 hold two wins and one loss. Every longer run is level or behind.
The whole period has 2 wins and 2 losses, which is level, so the best run is the first three days.
A day of exactly £0 is not a win, so no run has more wins.

tests.call: longest_winning_stretch([-1 if i % 3 else 1 for i in range(100000)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: A run wins when the running score rises across it, so look up the first day each score appeared.
When the score is not positive, the earliest score one below it gives the longest win; lower scores are reached later, as the score moves in steps of one.
One pass with a dict of first positions, so $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.
